On platforms like Newbook, models run job search, contracts and payments through an app, and payment is processed after the job is completed. That suggests reporting a completed job is a routine digital step.

Vendors say telecom AI agents connect to billing systems, explain charges and apply simple credits or adjustments on their own. Disputes that need judgment or regulatory handling are still passed to humans.

A 2026 telecom billing-agent deck limits the agent to 'approved billing intents' as a guardrail and reports about a 20% drop in billing support calls. That points to partial rather than full automation.

For third-number billing, an operator must check that the billed party agrees to pay (for example, asking whether a called party accepts a collect call). Older patents say collect and third-number calls had not been fully automated. Speech-recognition systems already handled parts of these calls.

Multi-carrier shipping platforms such as Shippo connect to more than 40 carriers, including USPS, UPS, FedEx and DHL. They compare rates and generate labels through a web app or an API. An agent could run this through a browser or the API and pick the shipping method.

Shipping software compares carrier rates in one dashboard, bulk-prints labels, and remembers package weights and dimensions. This automates the software side of deciding how to ship and preparing postage.

Rate-shopping engines built on aggregators such as EasyPost, ShipStation or Shippo apply the shipper's carrier rules automatically and create labels by API. A person still has to weigh, pack, label, bundle and hand over the physical items. This last point is my inference; the page does not say it.

Optical sorting machines like TOMRA's Sentinel II and 5A already reject defects and foreign matter (stones, plastic, glass, rot, discoloration) on the line. They do it with cameras and NIR sensors plus mechanical air ejectors, which is dedicated machinery. A software-only AI agent can't do this.

The TOMRA 5A lets operators adjust accept/reject levels through software and sends sorter data to the TOMRA Insight cloud. That is the only digital part of the work an agent could touch. Picking items off the belt and putting good product into containers is still physical handling.
Combined NIR and color sorters on root crops can handle up to 100 tons per hour. This shows that automating the task depends on physical equipment, not on an AI agent working through software.

Research on fault detection for combine harvesters uses vibration, acoustic and strain sensors with machine-learning classifiers. This shows AI can find faults from sensor data, but only when instrumented hardware is installed on the machine.

Predictive maintenance systems in agriculture use AI to compare sensor readings (vibration, temperature, pressure, torque) against a normal baseline and flag problems. This can support the operator's own monitoring by eye and ear, but it does not replace it.

John Deere collects sensor data from harvesters, tractors and planters and is adding computer vision and machine learning. The documented uses are mainly catching wrong settings, not judging machine sounds. The human operator in the cab is still the main detector.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178(l), only trained operators whose competence has been evaluated may drive powered industrial trucks (forklifts). Employers must certify that each operator has had the training and re-evaluate them at least every three years.

Industry guidance for grain, feed and processing operations treats forklift use as hands-on work by a human operator. The training has to cover the hazards specific to the site, which here means the auger and hopper area.

OSHA's 1998 final rule requires both formal instruction and practical exercises for anyone who drives a forklift, including workers who only do it as part of another job. The work is physical, so an agent that acts only through software cannot do it.

Field and bin scale systems already log each weighing digitally with picker RFID, date, time, weight and GPS. That leaves recording as the only digital sub-step, and a person still has to put the containers on the scale.
Libra Field Bin is an app that connects to bin load cells and logs each unload with weight, date, time and GPS, so the record-keeping is software-driven.

Weighmaster licensing in states like New York and California applies to issuing certified weight tickets for commercial or bulk sales. It generally does not cover routine on-farm weighing by equipment operators.

Remote water-level monitors (Farmbot) send tank and trough levels and rainfall data into AgriWebb's livestock software. An agent could read these dashboards and send alerts or reorder feed and water. That covers only the monitoring sub-step, and only on farms that have the sensors installed.

Automated feeding and drinking systems use level sensors, microcontrollers and apps to track supplies. The feeding and watering itself is still done by physical equipment or by workers, not by a software agent.

Systems that track drinking behaviour, such as RF-tagged water fountains, need hardware on site. Delivering feed, filling troughs, checking for frozen or broken waterers and seeing the animals in person all require someone physically there.

Maintenance happens by hand at the work site. The saw must be cooled, then the chain and bar cleaned and greased, for example every 3 days, and the chain brake kept working. An agent without a body cannot do any of this.
Sharpening means filing each cutter by hand at the correct angle with a file holder, after cleaning the chain and checking it for damaged teeth. All of it is hand work with tools.
Logging workers learn chainsaw sharpening and maintenance in hands-on courses, which shows these are physical skills with no software substitute.

OSHA's logging standard 29 CFR 1910.266 covers manual felling, chain saw use and machine use such as skidders as physical activities on the logging site. Its paragraph (i) requires training for workers who run chain saws and log skidders.
OSHA has an interpretation letter saying log skidder operators must be trained under 1910.266(i)(3)(ii). This is a training duty on the employer. It does not require a licensed human signature.

The University of Wisconsin Extension logging eTool describes chain saw felling and grapple skidder work as hands-on equipment work done in the woods. A software-only agent could not do any part of it.

Plasser & Theurer's ALC automatic guiding computer controls lining and levelling on tamping machines. This automation is built into the machine itself and is not something a general-purpose AI agent can take over through software. An operator on board still runs the machine and handles its reference systems.

Correction values for the precision method are calculated in advance and fed to the guiding computer. That digital pre-calculation is the only part of the job that sits close to what a software agent could do. Turning wheels and working levers on the machine is physical work.
Inside the machine, lining and levelling are measured against steel chords, and outside it against a laser. Both have to be set up and adjusted physically at the track.

Commercial core-image tools (ALS LithoLens, Seequent Imago) semi-automate lithology logging from photos and produce measurements such as RQD and fracture counts. Geologists still review and correct the results before they enter the geological record.

Image-based machine learning can classify lithology and alteration from core images, but results depend on photos taken on site and on lighting and image quality. Someone has to physically collect and photograph the cuttings or core at the rig.

In several US states, the licensed or registered well driller must keep a log of each stratum and file it with the state within 30 days of completion, so the driller stays accountable for the formation record.

AI field-service tools can schedule appointments, plan routes and pull device error logs remotely before a visit. A human technician still has to go to the home and do the repair, with remote help available at most.
Salesforce's field-service AI handles scheduling and dispatch and offers remote help for onsite technicians. It does not do the physical repair.

California requires businesses that repair TVs and audio-video equipment for pay to register as electronic service dealers. This is a business registration and does not say a human has to sign off on each job.

Machinists sharpen end mills by hand. They clamp the cutter in a collet fixture and grind it against a bench grinder wheel, then index each flute in turn and finish with a diamond hone. All of this is physical work that software alone cannot do.
Reconditioning carbide and coated cutters carefully takes an experienced technician working at a benchtop grinding machine. Physical skill is the core of the job.

Hobbyist machinists describe grinding end mills by hand on a lathe, using a rotary tool and marked chuck positions. No step of the work is done in software, so an agent could only help by looking up details such as grind angles or tool specifications.

The right pressing heat depends on the garment's fiber content and finish. For blends, use the setting for the fiber that tolerates the least heat. Pressers often press a test scrap and compare it with unpressed fabric, so the check is hands-on and done by eye and feel. AI can give this kind of rule-based advice from care-label or fiber data.

Charts matching fabric types to industrial press machines and heat settings already exist. An AI agent could look up and apply them when fiber data is available, but the presser at the station still has to inspect the garment and choose the machine.
Some sources give conflicting temperature figures, so a quick physical test on the actual fabric is still standard practice. That keeps a human in the loop for the final choice.

Pressing involves misting fabric by hand with a spray bottle or using a dampened press cloth before applying heat. This is physical handling of the garment, and a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do it.

Extension guidance says to test the moisture and heat on a hidden area first and to use a dampened press cloth when the fabric can't take steam. These are hands-on judgments made while touching the fabric, not digital steps.
Water relaxes natural fibers so wrinkles press out, which means the task itself is putting water physically onto the textile.

O*NET lists this task for Pressers (51-6021.00): workers select, install and adjust pressing forms, rollers and guides using hoists and hand tools. The work is hands-on mechanical setup, which an AI agent with no body cannot carry out. At most it could look up a manual or a part number.

Other duties in the same occupation are also physical: setting heat and pressure on the machine controls and finishing garments with hand irons. This shows the job is done at the machine, not through software.
O*NET lists Sewers, Hand (51-6051.00) duties as physical handling of fabric: aligning parts, basting and joining material by hand with needle and thread. No software tool performs these steps.
The occupation is entered with little formal education and needs no licence, so no law requires a human to perform or sign the work. The barrier is purely physical manipulation of material.

Upholstery estimating tools exist that calculate yardage, labor and materials and produce PDF quotes. A vendor guide claims a vision model estimated yardage from photos to within about one yard roughly 80% of the time on standard pieces, but it struggles with curved, tufted or vintage pieces, so the upholsterer still checks yardage and sets prices.

AI reupholstery visualizers can show customers how candidate fabrics would look on their furniture, which covers part of the fabric, color and style discussion. The tool's article could not be read, so its fabric-swap handling is unverified.

About 9 states plus D.C. license upholstery businesses, with fees but no exams. These are business licenses and do not require a licensed person to carry out or sign the customer consultation or estimate.

Slab-nesting and DXF-template software for countertop fabricators (e.g., SlabWise) automates turning templates into layouts and machine-ready files, but by the vendor's own account it does not deal with physical stone features like veining and remnants.
General AI nesting tools such as Nest&Cut automatically lay out shapes from DXF input to save material.
Machine-learning pipelines that read dimensions from engineering drawings reach about 81% accuracy, so critical dimensions still need a human to check them.

This task is done in person in the cargo hold during flight: inspecting restraints, watching for cargo shifting, smoke or leaks, then reporting to the pilots and taking corrective action. An agent with no body can't do these.
The loadmaster is a member of the flight crew. In-flight duties include visually checking interior and exterior clearances, running in-flight checks from the flight manual, and monitoring cargo.

Military loadmaster duties also include monitoring aircraft systems (fuel, hydraulic, electrical, environmental) and air traffic control radio while on board. These are crew-member responsibilities for a qualified person who is physically present. This source covers military roles, so it is only a rough guide to civil operations.

Factories do automate dosing. When manual addition is replaced, the work goes to dosing tanks and digital pumps, which are fixed hardware and not a software AI agent. The manual version needed extra manpower and physical handling of the chemicals.

In automated powder dosing, an operator types ingredient ratios and recipes into an HMI and a PLC controls the feeders. This setup screen is the only part a software agent could plausibly touch, and it depends on plant control systems that agents normally cannot reach.

Manual systems depend on an operator adding the chemicals by hand. Automated systems use sensors, controllers and pumps. Either way the task is physical or done by machinery, so a bodiless AI agent can only help with things like calculating amounts or looking up procedures.

In practice, operators run chemical tests by hand on water at the plant using chlorine titrators, pH meters and turbidity meters, then adjust chemical feeds. This is physical sampling and instrument work.
O*NET lists 'Test materials and solutions, using testing equipment' as a task for Pump Operators, Except Wellhead Pumpers, next to collecting samples and adding chemicals to tanks.

Online analyzers can feed SCADA continuously. Under EPA Method 334, they can be used for compliance only alongside regular manual grab-sample checks, so an agent can only help with reading data, interpreting it and keeping records.

Farm payroll platforms already handle blended piece-rate and hourly pay, minimum-wage top-ups, H-2A compliance, housing deductions and mobile time capture. That covers the main calculation and processing steps, which an agent can run through software.

Under 29 CFR 500.81, a farm labor contractor must pay wages when due and at least every two weeks (or semi-monthly). The law sets what must be paid and when, but it does not require a person to do the payroll work. The contractor is still legally liable, and a human usually approves the money going out.

MSPA requires an itemized written wage statement for each worker every pay period, including the employer's IRS EIN. Software can generate this automatically, but the hours and piece counts behind it come from crew leaders in the field. Many seasonal workers are also paid by paper check or cash handed out in person.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1926.451, scaffolds may only be put up, moved, taken down or altered by trained workers supervised by a qualified competent person. That person has to judge on site whether the footing is adequate and fit ties or braces to stop tipping, so a person must physically be there.

A competent person must inspect each scaffold for visible defects before every shift and after any event that could affect its structural integrity. These are hands-on checks done in person, and the law puts the responsibility on a human.

OSHA's standard interpretations cover how scaffold and ladder access is physically erected and secured. The task is moving, placing and anchoring heavy equipment on a job site, which a software-only agent with no robotics cannot do. My search did not separately check the ladder or hoist rules.
Sarine's machine-learning Clarity system maps diamond inclusions and blemishes. It needs dedicated imaging hardware with the physical stone placed in it.
GIA and IBM Research built an automated clarity grading system trained on tens of millions of graded diamonds. It was in limited use at GIA labs, covering only the most popular sizes at first.
Automated grading depends on hardware, lighting and stone orientation. A software-only agent cannot do that physical setup or the loupe and microscope examination.

Royal IHC's dredging control system monitors and automates slurry pumps, gate valves and suction pipes. Its pump controller prevents pipeline clogging. This is onboard vessel automation run by the crew, not a general AI agent working through software.

Dragflow's Pumping Control System runs from a handheld tablet next to the equipment. It monitors density, flow and pressure and can switch components on and off. Line flushing still needs an operator on site to set valves and check that the pipeline is clear.

Automatic hopper-dredge controls start the pump with the overboard discharge valve open. These sequences are built into vessel control systems, which an outside software agent would not normally be able to reach.

NCSL's preliminary 2026 survey: 55% of legislative staff use generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and Claude. They use them for research, summarizing, transcribing meetings and some drafting. Staff are still told to verify all output, and nothing describes AI doing the negotiating.

Lawyers in the US House Office of Legislative Counsel are spending more time fixing AI-drafted bills with errors. In South Dakota, a lawmaker had Grok write first drafts of a bill that was later folded into a compromise package, but the senators still negotiated it themselves.

Lawmaking in 2026 is adopting AI for drafting and analysis support, while the actual bargaining between legislators and parties happens through human relationships, often face-to-face and behind closed doors.

Under TSA's checked-baggage process, CT explosive detection systems flag bags automatically. A TSO then reviews the images and decides whether to clear the bag or open it. Physical inspections are done by hand, on camera, and the officer leaves a Notice of Inspection in the bag.

Workers log every bag they physically handle, including who opened it and when. Fewer than 10% of bags are touched. Spotting tampering means handling and looking at the bag itself, which needs a human.

AI threat-detection tools for CT images (Pangiam/Project DARTMOUTH, SeeTrue) are in TSA trials. They are purpose-built vendor systems that help with image screening, not general software agents, and they do not physically check bags for tampering.

Gym maintenance software such as UpKeep and BlueFolder already handles the arranging side of the job: logging problems through QR codes, scheduling preventive maintenance by usage or date, assigning work orders to outside vendors, and keeping asset and warranty records. An agent could run these steps end to end.

The maintenance itself is hands-on. Job postings describe inspecting, cleaning, lubricating and tightening machines, checking electrical connections, and lifting equipment over 50 lb, so a person has to be there.

Postings ask for CPR/AED and sometimes OSHA training, but no licence requires a human to do or sign off fitness equipment maintenance. A person still has to inspect the machines and do or check the repairs.
Vendor gym software says its AI reads member preferences, usage and attendance data to suggest new class offerings and forecast how renewals and class participation affect revenue.
TeamUp says it launched an AI Business Advisor: a monthly report built from a studio's own performance data and industry benchmarks that recommends business actions.

A vendor example shows AI spotting that evening yoga classes keep filling up and prompting the gym to add sessions or hire instructors. Analysis and recommendations can be automated, but approving the offering and committing budget remains a human management decision.

AI dosing systems already exist: CURATE.AI generated individualised capecitabine dose recommendations, and clinicians accepted close to 97% of them in a 10-patient pilot. Clinicians still made the final call.

Under 21 CFR 312.60 the investigator is accountable for running the study according to the protocol and for protecting subjects. FDA guidance says the investigator stays responsible for any task delegated to staff, so a physician must review and decide on any dose change an agent advises.

Duties on clinical research teams are split by role: coordinators support and document under the investigator's oversight, while clinical decisions such as dose changes stay with qualified investigators.

Clinical trial management software (CTMS) already works out each subject's protocol visit dates and windows, warns when a window is about to close or a visit is overdue, and texts subjects confirmations and reminders automatically. This covers the routine calculation and reminder parts of the task.

Once a protocol visit schedule is assigned to a subject in a CTMS, the system predicts when each visit should happen. A visit outside its window is a protocol deviation, so a human still has to judge edge cases and documentation.

AI scheduling agents that find open slots and book through Epic FHIR APIs exist but are mostly at proof-of-concept stage. Booking procedures and inpatient stays in hospital electronic health record systems depends on integration and permissions, and an agent often won't have that access.

In a Nov 2025 arXiv prototype, an agentic inventory system handled forecasting, supplier selection and negotiation in a mid-sized store. Against baseline heuristics it cut stockouts and holding costs and improved product-mix turnover. This was a prototype, not a live deployment.

A June 2026 industry description says agentic AI uses ERP data, supplier portals and logistics APIs to optimize inventory on its own. These are vendor claims, and no independent field data on inventory turns was found.

Supply-chain agents check stock against lead times and safety stock. They order on their own only within set authority limits and send larger decisions to humans for approval, so a human still signs off on major changes.

Vendors describe AI design-compliance agents that read specifications, drawings and regulatory documents, check designs against standards, flag likely violations and produce structured compliance reports. Vendors present them as first-pass reviewers, with engineers keeping the final judgment.
Florida DEP requires remedial action plans and engineering documents to be prepared by, or under the direct supervision of, a Florida-registered professional engineer, who must seal and sign them.
New Mexico requires a professional engineer to design and seal final remediation plans that include engineered systems such as mechanical or electrical equipment.

Industry sources describe AI agents in 2026 that read inbound carrier emails, pull out lane, rate and capacity details, send quote requests and place voice calls to carriers. Vendors claim 60-94% no-touch automation. Edge cases that depend on relationships, such as capacity crunches or negotiating favors, still go to humans.
C.H. Robinson's Navisphere real-time rating calls carrier APIs with a standard payload, and carriers return rates automatically. No human contact is needed for routine rate and schedule requests.
Loadsmart's API inside the Kuebix TMS returns instant, bookable truckload spot quotes. Asking carriers for rates is already a software-to-software step.

Vendors in 2026 sell AI and agentic tools that scan EDC and other trial data for discrepancies and draft queries. In each case a data manager approves or rejects the results, so the human keeps final review. These claims come from vendor marketing.
Clinion describes a multi-agent setup: one agent reads the protocol and case report forms, and another flags discrepancies and drafts queries. Clinion won the ACDM 2025 innovation award.

This is a secondary summary, not the primary text. Under ICH E6(R3), a responsible party must set the scope of audit-trail and data review on a risk basis and document it. Data corrections must be attributed and justified. This calls for human accountability, but no licence or law requires a human to perform each QC check. QC work runs inside validated, access-controlled GxP systems.

Agentic HEC-RAS is an MCP server for Claude Code and Codex built on the open-source ras-commander library. It lets an agent inspect, edit, run, read, compare and plot 1D/2D HEC-RAS models from a plain-language goal without opening the GUI. The author says it was checked end to end on HEC's Muncie 2D example. This is a self-description and I found no independent test.

RAS Commander is an MIT-licensed Python library that automates HEC-RAS plan runs, HDF result extraction and geometry operations. Its documentation says it was developed with LLMs including Claude and GPT-4. The search did not show whether agents can reliably build and calibrate a model from scratch, rather than edit an existing one.

Under 44 CFR 65.7, all analyses submitted to FEMA must be certified by a registered professional engineer. Floodway no-rise certifications must also be signed and sealed by a PE. So for regulatory flood models, a human engineer has to review and take responsibility for the work.

Enphase's Solargraf says its AI-assisted tool builds complete permit plan sets, including single-line and three-line diagrams, in under 10 minutes. It also says the tool pulls NEC code automatically and exports DWG files. These are vendor claims, so the drafting steps can be automated by software that an agent can operate.

Solargraf generates single-line, three-line and detailed calculation pages that it describes as permit-ready. No independent check of how accurate they are or how often permit offices accept them was found, so an engineer still needs to review them against the NEC and local rules.

Some permit offices require a single-line diagram stamped by an electrical engineer, for example when a line-side PV connection modifies electrical distribution equipment. Engineering documents for larger systems often need a PE stamp, so a human has to sign off.

In 2026, PNNL's AutoLabs multi-agent LLM system wrote chemical procedures for a liquid-handling robot and corrected its own errors, reaching an F1-score above 0.89 on multi-step syntheses. This shows agents can handle protocol and experiment-design sub-steps, though the authors also describe limits.

Self-driving labs, such as NC State's catalyst lab, design, run and analyze iterative chemistry experiments with little human input. Researchers note that true experimental autonomy is still limited and that the field has not settled on what 'autonomous' means.

Interactive robot training relies on kinesthetic teaching, where a person physically guides the robot, or on human teleoperation with VR controllers or spacemice. These demonstrations require a human operator with the physical robot.

A Japan Science and Technology Agency (CRDS) study from August 2026 describes specialized AI agents that split research work while another AI coordinates the overall research process. These are mostly prototype systems. They support coordination but have not replaced how human scientists coordinate with each other.

Coordinating interdisciplinary research is still advertised as a human role. A 2026 Know-Center job posting asks a postdoc to coordinate scientific collaboration across an interdisciplinary team, which relies on interpersonal trust and scientific judgment.

Writing about AI research agents in 2026 presents them as partners that speed up searching, drafting and analysis. They are not described as independently negotiating collaborations, dividing work between scientists or aligning their priorities.

OpenEduCat sells an AI lesson-plan generator for PE. Its marketing says it produces inclusive stations, changes difficulty through distance, ball size or target size, and adds modification notes and progressions. That covers drafting the planning step, which is only part of the task.

A practitioner guide for special education teachers presents AI as a drafting assistant for adapting lessons. Teachers have to review, verify and personalize every output and remain responsible for what reaches students.

Some states require a licensed physical educator to deliver adapted PE services. Wisconsin requires an adaptive PE license, and Connecticut requires a certified physical educator to serve students with IEPs. Adapting instruction means watching motor performance and adjusting it live in the gym.

The ASA 2008 Pre-Anesthesia Checkout Recommendations list 15 items to check each day or after the machine is moved or serviced, and 8 items before each procedure. Machine-builtin automated checkout covers only some of these steps; it is device firmware, not a general AI agent.

APSF reports a machine that passed its automated self-test and still failed during ventilation. It recommends a manual functional test of the breathing circuit and ventilator, using the breathing bag as a test lung, so physical hands-on work is still required.

Automated self-tests check internal transducers and circuit compliance. They cannot replace manual checks of vaporizers, suction, cylinder reserves and backup bag-valve devices (secondary study-guide source).

Harvesting cultures for cytogenetic analysis is a manual, multi-step bench process that averages two to three hours. The automation that exists is lab hardware (harvesters, metaphase spreaders, stainers), not software agents.

Automated harvesters such as the HANABI-PIII handle blood and bone marrow suspension cultures by physical robotics. A human still loads and handles the specimens, and a software-only AI agent cannot do these steps.

Cytogenetic technologists who process patient specimens and perform tissue culture must meet the CLIA high-complexity testing personnel requirements (42 CFR 493 Subpart M), and employers often also require ASCP CG certification.

FDA-cleared AI for digital cytology (Hologic Genius Digital Diagnostics / Genius Cervical AI) only triages cervical Pap slide images for a cytotechnologist or pathologist to review. It is a specialised device, not a general agent, and it does not do hormonal or maturation-index evaluation.

Under CLIA, 42 CFR 493.1274, individual cytology screeners must examine the slides, with a cap of 100 slides per person in 24 hours and records of each person's workload. This means a licensed human must do the screening and be accountable for it.

The digital workflow still needs glass slides to be physically prepared, stained and scanned, or examined under a microscope. A general software agent would usually not have access to lab scanners or the LIS.

AI articulation apps (Sara for SLP, SpeechLP, TikTalk) can run practice drills that the SLP sets up and give automatic error feedback. They cover only home or drill practice, not full treatment sessions.
SLPAs carry out specific parts of care plans written by an SLP, under supervision. The supervising SLP keeps full legal and ethical responsibility.
State law (Illinois) defines the assistant's role as carrying out the SLP's documented treatment plan under supervision. Assistants may not work with clients outside that plan.

Esri's ArcGIS now has agentic AI. External agents can connect to ArcGIS tools over MCP/A2A, run geoprocessing tools and complete multi-step GIS workflows with little user input. AI assistants also write ArcPy/Arcade code.
AI-generated ArcPy scripts for GIS automation often fail on the first try and need a human to debug them. That means a human still has to review the work before it is used.

As of 2026, US intelligence agencies are still working to get agentic AI onto classified networks, where accreditation is a very high bar, and officials say humans will keep making key decisions. This limits an agent's access to the databases analysts normally use.

Critical event management platforms such as OnSolve use AI risk intelligence to scan many data sources, flag events like severe weather, estimate their impact on people and operations, and send multi-channel alerts. These are the monitoring and notification steps of the task.

Rave Mobile Safety lets retail staff send mass notifications by email, text, digital signage and broadcast, and links incident administrators with first responders. Its materials describe retail stores as highly susceptible to violence, active shooter events, outages and weather-related closures.

Retail incident case management tools such as Appriss Retail Incident handle evidence capture, alerts and documentation. The response itself still happens on site: securing the store, evacuating people and working with police.

Connected spa systems like SmartTub can remotely detect power failures, GFCI trips, heater malfunctions, open covers and nearby moisture, and send alerts through an app. This is the part of the work an agent could monitor through software.

Patents for remote spa control describe sensors that track temperature, turbidity and chemical levels and raise alerts when they detect a fault. This sensor data is the only equipment check that happens digitally; the rest needs someone on site.
Remote diagnostics only flag problems. A person still has to inspect and test the equipment on site, including saunas, steam rooms, massage tables and treatment devices.

Customs iX's Classify module suggests HS codes with duty rates and preference eligibility, and its 2026 release adds declaration generation. Vendors also say OCR models pull entry data from invoices, packing lists and bills of lading.

Vendor sources describe a hybrid workflow: AI proposes classifications and declarations, and a human reviews them before filing. The accuracy figures they give come from vendor blogs and have not been independently verified.

In the US, 19 CFR Part 111 governs broker licences and permits, including the rules for doing customs business without a licence. Since the 2022 rule, a brokerage firm must employ enough licensed brokers to keep its customs work under responsible supervision and control. This points to a human with legal responsibility for clearance filings.

Under the IRC, every penetration through the roof plane must be flashed. Installers generally fit flashing according to the roofing manufacturer's printed instructions. This is hands-on work done on the roof.

Michigan's rooftop PV rule requires penetrations to be flashed and sealed following the manufacturer's instructions. The cited version was listed as effective until 8/29/2025, so it may no longer be current. It describes code requirements for the work, not a rule that only a licensed person may do it.
Penetrations sealed only with mastic or silicone are not considered durable, so flashing devices have to be physically installed around the hole.

Research agent systems such as MetaChat (Stanford) and VortexChat turn photonic design goals written in plain language into device designs by running simulate-and-iterate loops. They are research prototypes, not turnkey products for deciding on applications.

OptiAgent's authors report that LLMs often fail to turn what they understand from text into workable optical designs without physics-based checks. That points to a continued need for human expert review.
A PE licence is generally needed only to sign and seal plans submitted to public authorities. Photonics R&D and product design work inside a company usually does not require a licensed signature.

Climate FieldView already builds zone-level variable-rate seeding prescriptions from historical yield data and satellite imagery, using known optimal seeding rates for commercial hybrids. An agent can drive this kind of software or reproduce the analysis in code, which covers the core GIS-to-prescription steps.

A patent family describes software that identifies management zones in a field and generates planting plans for each zone. It can use a yield-based model (seed hybrid, target yield, historical yield) or an economics-based model, and the two can give different recommendations. Choosing between them and checking them against local agronomic knowledge still takes human judgement before use.

No law was found that requires a licensed or Certified Crop Adviser to make seeding-rate or variety recommendations. The licensing rules found in Arizona, Louisiana and California apply to pesticide advice and nitrogen management plans instead.
OCLC WorldShare Acquisitions can claim serial issues automatically through saved searches and scheduled jobs. Claims only go out when a vendor contact email is set.
SirsiDynix Symphony serial control produces claim notices for missing issues as reports and can send EDI claims to vendors that are set up for EDI.

In Voyager-style workflows, check-in patterns flag missed issues into a problem file that staff review before claiming. This includes physically confirming whether an issue arrived but was not checked in.

When payment systems are connected to the hotel's property management system (PMS), payment events are sent to the PMS automatically and the guest's bill updates without staff input. Refunds update it the same way.

Charges from linked systems such as point of sale, minibar and spa are posted to the guest's bill automatically through PMS interfaces. When systems use different identifiers, posts fail and staff have to clean them up by hand.

A vendor says its AI agents match card batches, cash and booking-channel payouts against PMS postings and keep an audit trail. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been independently checked. A PMS records a charge but does not prove the money was collected, so a human still has to review discrepancies and count the cash.

AI rehabilitation apps such as MED-EL ReDi and Neurotone LACE AI Pro already run personalized listening, speechreading and speech-in-noise training on their own. These are sub-steps of the instruction part of the task, though the claims come mostly from the vendors.

ASHA places aural rehabilitation for adults, including counseling, within the scope of licensed audiologists and SLPs, who are expected to be specifically trained for it. State practice acts define it as licensed audiology practice.

Trade guidance says AI training apps work best when the clinician frames them as rehabilitation and persuades patients to take part. That keeps the person-to-person counseling and motivation with a human.

The machines that do automate sandwich, bowl, salad and drink prep are dedicated robots (Nala Robotics Sandwich Bot and Bowl Bot, Rolo Robotics micro kitchens). That is physical hardware, not a software AI agent without a body.

Even 2026 automated micro kitchens do the frying, baking, salad and beverage work with physical modules. The task is hands-on handling of food, so an agent that acts only through software cannot do it.
The FDA Food Code requires a designated Person in Charge on site during operation, but no licence requires a specific person to do the food prep itself. The decisive barrier is physical, not legal.
AI feedback agents for dine-in guests open from a QR code on a table tent, check presenter or receipt. They collect satisfaction feedback in the guest's phone browser.

A restaurant feedback chatbot vendor says its bot passes serious complaints to staff with the conversation history and does not try to resolve them itself. Humans still handle the in-person resolution.
POS-linked and QR survey platforms such as Ovation detect negative sentiment in real time and route it to managers so staff can act during or after the visit.

Vendors say their camera-based AI can read container codes, track crane and grab states, and check load sequences against stowage plans. These are claims, not independent tests, and the systems run on fixed port or crane cameras, not on the ship officer's watch.
The master holds overall responsibility for cargo stowage. Supervision is usually delegated to the chief officer, who watches loading on deck and in the holds.
The master must make sure the approved Cargo Securing Manual is followed strictly. Only people with practical knowledge of that manual may take charge of stowage.

Stocking shelves means physically moving and placing goods. Shelf-stocking robots are dedicated robotic hardware, not software agents. Salling Group's October 2026 humanoid trial needs human operators to guide every movement.
Telexistence's TX SCARA restocks beverage shelves in Japanese convenience stores, but it is a physical robot rather than a software agent, and remote humans take over when it fails.
Software and AI help mostly with monitoring, such as shelf-scanning systems that report stock gaps. The physical placement of goods still falls to human associates.

ERP storeroom modules can create a pick list automatically when an approved requisition is released. This step tells the storeroom to start issuing items, but staff still have to issue them physically and then confirm the pick.

In asset-management software, the user builds pick lists from work orders or requisitions and issues the parts. The system then records the transactions and assigns costs, so the agent's share is the digital paperwork, not taking material out of the warehouse.

Pick processing includes physically retrieving items, checking them with barcode or RFID scans, and deducting them from inventory. The retrieval and hand-over steps need someone physically present, which an AI agent without a body cannot do.

OSHA 29 CFR 1910.22 requires storerooms, passageways and floors to be kept clean, orderly and free of hazards such as spills and protruding objects. Meeting it means physically sweeping, wiping, removing obstructions and inspecting the space.

Floor cleaning in warehouses is being automated by physical robots, such as Brain Corp's BrainOS scrubbers. Those are robotic hardware, which this rating excludes. A software-only agent can only draft cleaning checklists, schedules or compliance logs.
OSHA lets employers decide how often walking-working surfaces are inspected, and no licence or human sign-off is required. The barrier here is physical, not legal.
Lucas Dynamic Slotting is a commercial tool that uses machine learning to assign storage slots. It works from SKU velocity, SKU affinity, product and slot attributes, and pick paths.
Infios AI runs inside a warehouse management system. It keeps analyzing pick frequency, velocity and affinity data, then recommends and carries out location reassignments.

Slotting software takes item demand, physical attributes, handling methods and storage constraints into account. Its output is an item-to-location assignment and a list of relocations for staff to carry out. A human still has to check physical and environmental conditions on site.

Accessory installs mean hands-on work: disconnecting the negative battery cable, removing cowls, connecting harnesses, securing them with wire ties and testing the lights. An AI without a body can't do any of that.
