evidence.fact: Harley-Davidson harness kits need physical tools such as a heat gun and a Deutsch terminal crimp tool. They also carry electrical limits like fuse amperage and wire gauge per splice. An AI could look these up and check them, but it can't carry them out.

The manufacturer's instructions are digital documents. Here an agent can help by finding the right procedure, checking fitment and adding up electrical load. No law requires a licensed person to do the install itself.

Funeral home management platforms such as The Smart Director already automate death certificate filing through state Electronic Death Registration Systems (EDRS) and track merchandise inventory, so an agent working through this kind of software could do most of the record work.

In Colorado, the funeral director or person acting as such who first takes custody of the body is responsible for filing the death certificate. Electronic submission counts as the signature, so accountability stays with a human filer.
Washington's EDRS requires each funeral director to get an identity-verifying digital certificate before filing, which limits direct agent access and keeps a human in the loop.

Vendors describe recruiting agents that source candidates by analyzing profiles and career signals. They also watch pipelines and, when a role falls behind, add sourcing channels or re-engage passive candidates on their own. Most deployments are still shallow (job descriptions, basic screening), and the autonomy claims come mainly from vendors.

Korn Ferry's 2026 Talent Acquisition Trends report says 52% of talent leaders plan to add AI agents to their teams. Recruiters' time is expected to shift toward turning hiring data into business strategy, so humans keep the strategic alignment and approval steps.

The EU AI Act classes recruitment AI as high-risk and requires human oversight; sources disagree on whether this applies from August 2026 or, under the AI Omnibus, December 2027. NYC Local Law 144 requires only bias audits and notice to candidates. Neither law requires a licensed human to write or sign off a recruiting strategy.

Blackbaud says its Development Agent, built into Raiser's Edge NXT, finds, cultivates and contacts donors, and that the platform surfaces recommended actions and donor briefings. This is a vendor claim.

DonorSearch Ai trains custom acquisition and retention models on an organization's own giving history and returns ranked prospect scores, which automates a core analytic step in planning for new or larger gifts.

Salesforce Nonprofit Cloud offers Agentforce-based fundraising agents, including a Prospect Research Agent. Strategy approval and how well it fits with relationships, the board and the mission still depend on humans.

SpeakUp, a speaker-matching platform, says it offers an MCP server that lets ChatGPT or Claude agents find, shortlist, contact and book speakers within a chat. This is the vendor's own claim and has not been independently checked.
Event-platform guides describe using AI to research speakers, draft personalized invitation emails and handle logistics, which covers most of the digital sub-steps of securing a speaker.

AI email agents can already send personalized outreach at volume and schedule follow-ups automatically. Choosing which speaker fits the cause, persuading high-profile or unpaid speakers through personal relationships, and committing to fees or contracts still need a human.

In low vision acuity testing, the examiner moves the patient closer to the chart (to 2 m, then 1 m) and uses single cards. With very poor vision, the examiner also counts fingers, checks hand motion and tests light perception. All of these need a person in the room handling materials and the patient.

Smartphone and at-home acuity tests (Peek Acuity, Vision at Home, and the three home tests compared in JAMA Ophthalmology 2022) came within about one line of in-office ETDRS results. But validation mostly involved people with normal or mildly impaired vision, and accuracy varied with the level of impairment. Software can therefore help with chart display, scoring and records, but it cannot replace in-person low vision and blindness testing.
A full low vision assessment covers history, acuity, refraction, contrast sensitivity, color vision, glare and visual fields, using physical charts and devices with the patient present.

Oracle Health's Clinical AI Agent for nurses is commercially available in the US. It writes short nursing summaries for shift handoffs from physician notes, medications, labs and orders. This covers the record-review part of gathering patient information.

Handoff-summary tools such as Pokee AI build summaries from notes, vitals, labs and care plans, but they keep the output as a draft until a nurse reviews it. The search found no tool built for nursing-assistant handoffs.

Nursing assistants work under a licensed nurse's delegation and follow the plan of care. Instructions from physicians or family go through the nurse. Much of the information comes from verbal report and huddles on the unit, and the aide has to understand it personally before giving care.

Hospital delivery robots such as Aethon TUG/ZenaRx and Relay carry specimens and medications with locked compartments and logged chain of custody. These are robots, and the reference technology has no robotics. A software agent could only handle the logging and tracking part.

Automated chain-of-custody software records who loaded and delivered each item, along with times and locations. This digitizes the documentation step, but someone still has to move the items physically.

Relay Robotics advertises secure autonomous transport with chain-of-custody tracking for medications and lab specimens. Even with these robots, the core of the task is physical handoff to authorized staff.

Under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(4)(iii), contaminated sharps have to go into closable, puncture-resistant, leakproof, labeled containers. These containers must be replaced routinely and not overfilled. Each of these steps is physical handling at the point of use.

Reusable sharps containers may not be opened, emptied or cleaned by hand or in any other way that puts workers at risk. Final disposal must follow federal, state and local regulated-waste rules, so the work is done by physically segregating and moving the material.

OSHA governs how waste is contained and handled where it is used, and state medical-waste and EPA rules govern what happens after that. Only small digital sub-steps, such as looking up the rules or filling in waste logs and manifests, could go to an AI agent with no body.

CLSI GP41-based practice puts the explanation at the bedside, just before the draw. It sits alongside spoken patient identification, implied consent (for example, the patient rolls up a sleeve after the explanation) and stopping if the patient withdraws consent. So the core explanation is an in-person exchange with the phlebotomist and is part of the draw.

CLSI says blood collection must not go ahead against the patient's consent and treats patient-centred communication as part of the collection procedure. This makes the explanation a trust and care step built into the physical procedure.

In lab medicine, AI chatbots are documented for explaining results and for scheduling blood tests. I found no products that give the bedside explanation of a collection procedure, so AI is limited to support work such as pre-visit instructions (fasting, urine or stool collection kits) and written handouts.

O*NET 51-5113.00 lists this task as a core task (importance 87). It is done by hand or with a machine: stitching or gluing endpapers, bindings, backings or signatures using sewing machines, glue machines, or glue and brushes.

The work includes forming book bodies by folding and sewing printed sheets into signatures and assembling them in order. These are hands-on, physical steps that a software-only agent with no robotic body cannot do.
The usual entry requirement is a high-school diploma. The occupation profile shows no licence or sign-off rule that would require a human to do the task.

VueScan's software automates dust and scratch removal using the scanner's infrared channel. Its auto-crop and auto white balance are meant to keep manual adjustment low when batch scanning slides and negatives, so an agent using a computer could run the scanning settings and post-processing.

Batch film scanners such as PowerFilm Plus still need a person to physically load the filmstrips (up to 10 strips of 6 frames per batch). After that, the scanner removes dust and scratches with infrared Magic Touch cleaning on its own, so handling the media remains a human step.

The Plustek OpticFilm 135i batch scans groups of up to 4 slides or 6 negatives and corrects dust with an infrared channel. Software handles the scanning, but someone must physically feed the film or slides into the machine.

Fleet telematics such as Kärcher Fleet and Diversey Taski IntelliTrail give managers each cleaning machine's run time, location and condition, and flag machines that need attention. An agent could read this data and schedule maintenance.

Janitorial Manager's equipment-tracking software records equipment location, usage and repair costs, and takes repair requests through QR codes. This covers the digital record-keeping part of the task, but the inspection and repair are still done by hand.

Preventive maintenance checklists for floor scrubbers and sweepers involve physical inspection: checking batteries, squeegees, brushes, hoses and filters. That needs a person on site, which an agent without a body can't do.

Procore's AI agents, sold as Digital Coworker packages, can turn site photos and voice notes into a draft daily log, flag schedule, sequencing and float risks, and handle RFI and site-safety tasks. Procore says human teams still review and approve everything.

Procore's May 2026 launch says its Digital Coworkers automate construction workflows inside the platform. This covers the paperwork and coordination around site management, not directing crews in person.

State licensing rules for engineers define 'responsible charge' as direct control, personal supervision and legal responsibility for engineering work. The licensee must review the work and approve, change or reject it.
AI tools like Realgram AI and PlanoHero can generate store-specific planograms and layout plans automatically. That covers only the planning step, not the physical build.
Leafio uses image recognition to check shelf photos against approved layouts. Store staff still take the photos and set up the products by hand.

O*NET lists the core task as setting up displays in store space using lighting, colors and props, along with building displays and maintaining props and mannequins. All of this is hands-on physical work.

Consumer apps such as Nail Health Scanner and Nails AI can score nail and cuticle condition from a photo. Only the assessment part is covered, it only gives information, and the vendors' accuracy claims have not been checked independently. None of these apps can remove dead skin or massage hands.
In states such as Tennessee, manicurists must finish about 600 hours of training and pass both a written and a practical exam before they can be licensed.
Licensed nail technicians do hands-on work on clients, including massaging the hands, feet, forearms and lower legs. This requires being physically present with the client.
In RV dealer and rental orientations, a person typically walks the customer through the vehicle and shows how its systems work. These sessions often last 40–60 minutes.

Video orientation courses already deliver standardized explanations of RV systems to customers. This shows that much of the explaining can be done with pre-made content rather than a technician on site.
AI agents built for the RV industry answer customer questions from brochures and spec sheets and route service requests. No dedicated AI tool for walking customers through RV systems was found.

With SCADA or DCS, operators can start and stop equipment such as pumps and motors from a central HMI. This makes remote software starts technically possible in automated plants. Controllers then send the start signals to actuators in the field.

SCADA HMI mimic screens show whether a pump is running and its flow, so the operator can confirm a start or switch the pump off. An agent could read these screens, but plant control systems are usually walled off from general IT and AI tools.

Centrifuge operator jobs are hands-on, on-site roles: pre-start walkdowns, local start buttons, checking guards, lubrication and valve settings, and watching vibration and noise after the start. These need physical presence that a bodiless agent cannot provide.

USDA ARS Yield Editor 2.0 automates yield-data cleaning, including flow-delay correction and removing overlapped end-row data. On 50 test maps, its automated cleaning was not significantly different from cleaning done by an expert.

GeoPard imports harvester yield data directly from John Deere Operations Center. It then cleans the data, including outlier removal and striping correction, and builds yield maps, so the whole process runs in software.

Automated methods such as Climate Corp's patent on expert filters plus spatial outlier detection generate accurate yield maps from raw monitor data. No licence or sign-off is needed, but a human usually checks for calibration and multi-combine problems.

Consumer AI pet-health assistants, including Daisy, PawHealth AI's Evie and Pack Pet Health (built on Gemini), already give owners care tips tailored to breed, age and history. They also triage cases and tell owners when to see a vet. Most accuracy claims come from the vendors themselves.

In a vendor-run blinded test with UK vets, a specialised AI triage tool scored 81% accuracy, against 69% for Gemini and 50% for ChatGPT. Quality is useful but still imperfect, so a human should review the advice.

State veterinary practice acts stop non-vets from diagnosing, recommending specific treatments or prescribing. General care advice from a caretaker (feeding, grooming, exercise, hygiene) does not need a licence, but advice must stay below the level of diagnosis.

AI vision at pack stations can confirm SKU, slot and orientation from overhead cameras and flag errors before sealing. This is dedicated camera-and-gantry hardware built into the line. It is not a software-only agent, and a human still handles the items.

Machine-vision systems inspect packaging for item counts, presence/absence and defects. They depend on installed cameras, lighting and line integration, so physical inspection needs either on-site hardware or a person handling the product.

Vendor material describes AI vision as best suited to checking count, presence and placement. Physical checks such as handling, opening containers and testing seals or weight stay with the human packer. No licence or legal sign-off requirement applies to this task.

Cisco, Microsoft and Zoom announced meeting agents in late 2025 that can take part in calls, for example updating tickets and finding files. A 2026 vendor review says most meeting AI is still a notetaker and does its work after the call, so agents do not yet represent a person in meetings.

Service-desk agents create, categorize, route and fully resolve some employee requests (one vendor self-reports 15-25% resolved end to end) and escalate the rest. Vendors say this extends to HR, finance and procurement requests.
Agentic ticketing systems pass exceptions to humans when judgment is needed. Handling complaints and representing the unit in person still depends on human negotiation, trust and attendance.

Vendor pages say AI compliance agents continuously test controls such as access reviews and configuration baselines. They also say these agents collect evidence from identity providers, cloud and ticketing systems, flag drift and keep audit trails, and that high-risk fixes need human approval. This covers the digital part of compliance monitoring.
Agents run on a schedule to monitor controls, gather evidence and fix configuration drift within guardrails set by people, with human approval for high-risk changes.

Under the NISPOM (32 CFR 117), organizations in the National Industrial Security Program must run their own self-inspections, including an insider threat self-assessment. DCSA checks that findings are documented and fixed. Physical items such as GSA security containers, Closed Area accreditation and alarm/intrusion detection upkeep need checking on site, and a named human official is responsible for the program.

Physical penetration tests of offices, plants and server rooms are done on site. Testers work in person under signed authorization and try tailgating, lock bypass and sensor bypass, and they test fire and cooling systems. None of this can be done through software alone.

Software and sensors can already monitor temperature, smoke, humidity and floods and send alerts automatically. An agent could review that data, the floor plans and natural-hazard data, and draft findings against frameworks such as ISO 27001 control 7.5.

The DISN facility STIG requires physical penetration testing at least once a year, recommends an outside tester and has results reported to the site commander. A person is expected to carry out the test and own its results.

ReqGenie is a GPT-based research prototype that runs text-based stakeholder interviews and turns them into requirements. In a preliminary test, its outputs compared well with two existing SRS documents. This suggests an agent can carry out the elicitation and summary steps on its own.
A 2026 study of multi-agent requirements generation still has stakeholders review and refine what the agents produce. Human sign-off on requirements is still essential.
Commercial requirements tools present AI as an assistant. It pulls out candidate requirements, flags ambiguities and suggests clarifying questions, while humans make the decisions about requirements.

AI change-detection tools combine aerial and satellite imagery with existing map data to flag areas that may have changed, so specialists review fewer places. Comparing new imagery against an existing map is being automated, but people still review the results.

Methods that turn features extracted from aerial images into vectors and compare them against existing map vectors to find mismatches are documented. Manual visual comparison by analysts remains the slow baseline.

Under state law, technical staff prepare survey and mapping work under a licensed surveyor in responsible charge, who seals the final product. The technician's comparison step itself does not need a licence, but a human reviews the final product.

A vendor (OpenEduCat) says its AI planner builds 5-day lesson plans with IEP goal alignment, accommodation notes and pacing for co-teaching and resource-room settings. It also says it flags curriculum months where a goal has no planned activity. These are the vendor's own claims and were not independently checked.

A small peer-reviewed study (Education Sciences, Aug 2025) found ChatGPT made IEP goals clearer and lesson plans more structured. Teachers said human oversight was needed to fit the plans to real classroom conditions.

State co-teaching guidance treats co-planning as a live meeting between the general and special education teachers. The meeting covers curriculum, student data, supports and who leads each part of the lesson. Planning time comes from state, district or union rules, not a federal IDEA requirement, and no rule requires a human signature for the plans.

Library policy work is mostly research and drafting: comparing peer libraries' policies, surveying common practice and writing staff- and patron-facing text. ALA's 2026 guide and WebJunction materials describe this as document work that an agent can largely do end to end.

Public library boards of trustees hold the legal authority to adopt policies, for example under Washington RCW 27.12.210. Adoption means first and second readings at a public meeting, public comment and a majority vote, so humans must approve the result.
Staff and legal counsel review a policy before it is adopted. Trustees set the policy and the librarian and staff carry it out, so building agreement with stakeholders stays a human job.

Kirkpatrick Partners says AI can create and refine Level 2 learning assessments and automate Level 1 surveys and feedback. It also says a human should check those AI outputs against the performance objectives, so a person still has to review before use.

Kirkpatrick Partners offers an 'AI-Powered Evaluation Specialist' certification built with UnDesto AI, with 2026 sessions. This shows AI-assisted design of evaluation tools is established practice. The course also covers bias, privacy and validity risks that call for human oversight.

Training-evaluation survey guides note that Level 3 (behavior) and Level 4 (results) measures depend on organization-specific performance data and stakeholder agreement. An agent can draft these instruments, but a human has to validate them in context.

Districts already run field-trip, yearbook and club fees through online portals such as SchoolCash Online. Parents pay by card or e-check, get automatic notices, and the money goes straight to the school's bank account, though many schools still accept cash and checks.

Under state auditor guidance, a teacher or coach who collects money has to use a pre-numbered receipt book and keep a list of cash and check payments. That makes the in-person handling of cash a physical, hands-on step, while the record-keeping is digital work an agent could do.

District procedures let elementary teachers collect small amounts of cash or checks from students. School policies require the cash to be stored securely and handed to the office, and ask for receipting, banking and reconciliation to be split between staff. These are internal controls, not licensing rules.

Free AI design tools such as Canva AI, Venngage and Pixa generate classroom labels, bin labels and bulletin-board letters for printing. Only the design and printable-file step can be done in software.
O*NET lists this as a core teaching assistant task: organizing and labeling materials and displaying students' work at eye level, which is physical work done in the classroom.

UK teaching assistant job descriptions describe preparing, mounting and presenting displays of pupils' work and laminating materials. These are hands-on duties with no licensing or sign-off requirement.

Special education paraprofessional job descriptions list hands-on help with toileting, diapering, feeding, lifting and repositioning students, and wheelchair assistance, as required by the student's IEP.
Aides do health procedures such as tube feeding, catheterization and suctioning when the school nurse delegates them, and they work under the direction of a teacher or administrator.

AI tools in special education mainly adapt materials, support communication and tutor students. Reviews say they support special educators and do not replace them, and that teachers need to oversee them.

SoundSwitch software analyses tracks in batches to build light shows automatically (AutoScripting) and keeps lighting in sync with the beat (Autoloops) through USB-DMX alongside Serato, Engine DJ and VirtualDJ. This means software can already handle much of the live light cueing.

US laser shows need an FDA variance under 21 CFR 1040.11(c). They must be under the direct and personal control of trained operators who are positioned where they can see all beam paths, so a human has to run the lasers.
The FDA has checked at events that laser operators hold an approved variance and follow its conditions.

Vendors describe AI that reads referral documents, ranks urgency, fills in EHR referral forms and tracks referral status. That covers the paperwork and coordination steps, but no peer-reviewed evidence shows an agent completing ED-to-specialist referrals end to end.
In a 2025 ED pilot, an AI tool (Mediktor) recommended referral to urgent care for 43.6% of 427 non-severe patients. Clinicians and patients still made the final decision.
Medicare allows only PECOS-enrolled physicians or non-physician practitioners, each with an individual NPI, to order or refer services. A licensed human therefore has to be the referring party.

Konica Minolta's commercial 'Positioning i' AI measures how far key positioning points deviate and grades radiographs as Acceptable, Tolerable, or 'Re-radiography must be considered'. This supports the reject/repeat decision but does not take the exposure.
GE's AI gives real-time mammography positioning feedback before exposure, with about 96% validation accuracy. A technologist still positions the patient and fires the exposure.
New York Public Health Law §3502 allows only licensed practitioners and licensed persons to apply ionizing radiation to human beings.

Under Crawford v. Washington, testimonial statements are barred unless the witness is cross-examined at trial or was unavailable after an earlier chance to cross-examine. So the officer who saw the events must testify under oath in person.

AI tools like Axon Draft One only write first drafts of reports from body-camera audio. The officer reviews and signs the report, and prosecutors want officers to stay responsible because they may have to testify about what they witnessed.
The COPS Office says AI report tools cannot parse or summarize the visual content of video. That limits AI to a supporting role in preparing evidence for testimony.
District procedure: the driver and trained safety monitors physically shut off the engine, set the brake, use extinguishers and supervise unloading of passengers on site.
Bus monitor policy: a monitor near the front takes authority if the driver is injured, shuts off the ignition and keeps passengers calm, which requires being in the bus.
Ohio Admin. Code 3301-83-15 sets out required emergency and evacuation procedures and drills, and only trained personnel may transport pupils.

Funeral-home AI chatbots handle logistics and questions about services, pricing and documents, often around the clock, and pass families to staff when needed. They serve as a supportive first contact, not a replacement for human comfort.
A funeral-industry source recommends using AI chatbots for supportive administration rather than counseling. It notes safety limits and that conversations with a chatbot are not confidential.
One funeral home added EverGrace.Ai, a voice chatbot described as empathetic, to help families with early planning. This is a single anecdote from a podcast description.

Florida's standard procedure says that once the cremation finishes, all remains must be taken out and the retort swept clean. The ID tag goes into the recovery tray, and the brushes and tools must be checked for bone fragments. All of this is hands-on work done by the operator.
Remains have traditionally been taken out of the chamber with handled tools such as rakes and brooms. The only automation found is mechanical equipment, not software or AI.
The bone fragments are left to cool and then collected by hand from inside the chamber. The job requires being physically at the cremator.
Municipalities are moving bid solicitation, receipt and contract management onto e-procurement platforms such as OpenGov, which gives an agent digital access to most of the paperwork.
Public-sector procurement vendors advertise AI-powered features, including automated bid tabulation and compliance support. These are the vendor's own claims, not independent evidence.

Municipal codes require the city clerk or a designee to open bids and publicly read them aloud at a set time and place, which can be done virtually. The award is made by the council, so a human still has to perform and sign off on key steps.

FarmKeep lets a manager assign chores such as feeding animals and cleaning water troughs to farm members, set up recurring routines and track them in calendar, list or kanban views. This is the digital core of the task, which an agent could run end to end.

Farmbrite supports team schedules, task-assignment notifications and tracking tasks for individual livestock. An agent could build and send rosters from goal specifications, but someone still has to check animal condition and crew availability on site.

AgriWebb pushes planned livestock tasks and feed records to workers' mobile task lists, so assignments can be fully digital where the crew uses the app. Many farm crews are still directed verbally at the barn.
AI livestock tools such as Gau Swastha, Betty and Jaguza only suggest likely diagnoses and treatment protocols from photos, questionnaires or sensors. Farmers or vets still carry out the treatment.
On-farm treatment plans have caretakers follow the veterinarian's or the label's directions. Staff trained on SOPs physically give the drugs to the animals.
Prescription animal drugs can be used or dispensed only within a valid veterinarian-client-patient relationship, so a licensed vet has to authorize the treatment.

Crew-and-equipment dispatch software such as B2W Schedule has an 'Equipment Move Planner' that sends text and email notices to drivers and transport crews. This shows the planning, scheduling and messaging parts of the task can be done entirely in software, which an agent could run end to end.
Farm labor scheduling tools handle crew transport to remote fields and shift timing. They only coordinate logistics. The supervisor still directs the dismantling and setup on site.

No-code farm tools build scheduling, equipment tracking and field logs from general parts. No product we found automates the on-site physical work of taking equipment apart and setting it up again, which still needs a person there.

No-code AI platforms such as FlyPix analyze satellite, aerial and drone images. They flag stress and anomaly hotspots, weeds, pests and gaps in crop stands, and produce geolocated scouting points and walking routes. This speeds up field inspection, but a person still has to collect the imagery and check the findings on the ground.

Drone Ag's Skippy Scout app runs AI analysis on drone photos to report green area index, crop cover and weed percentage. The farmer has to fly the drone, so field inspection is only partly digitized and still depends on someone being there.

Tools that interpret drone imagery are reported to be about 10 times faster than walking crops. They cover crop fields, not checks of buildings, fences, supplies or equipment, which still need someone on site to look and handle things.

AI progress-monitoring tools (DroneDeploy Progress AI, OpenSpace, Buildots) read drone and 360° site imagery and compare it with the schedule. They depend on someone in the field capturing that imagery, so an agent can help with tracking but cannot do the on-site oversight.

Irrigation installs need on-site inspections, operational demonstrations and as-built checks. A licensed irrigator signs, dates and seals the completion certificate. That licence duty falls on the installer, not the farm supervisor.
From 2026, San Antonio's water utility (SAWS) requires a licensed person to supervise new irrigation installs and inspects each one on site. Physical presence is central to this kind of oversight.

Transplanting and potting are automated only with dedicated physical machinery, such as vacuum or gripper transplanters and mobile robots that move container-grown plants. A software-only AI agent cannot do this work.
Patents for automatic transplanting describe physically moving plugs and seedlings from one container to another. The task is mainly hand work with plants and soil.
Patents describe autonomous mobile robots that carry container-grown plants to stations for re-potting, grading and sorting. Robotics is required, which the reference agent does not have.

AI agent templates already take plant orders from start to finish: they help customers pick plants, take payment and collect delivery details. That covers the digital selling step. Loading plants and handing them over still needs a person.

An online garden center put an AI agent on its repetitive customer questions about delivery costs and times. The vendor claims this saved about one full-time employee, a figure that has not been independently checked.
States require a nursery or plant dealer license to sell rooted plants. The license belongs to the business, not to the worker, so no human has to sign off on each sale or delivery.

O*NET lists mending fences and farm buildings as part of this occupation's work. A DOL H-2A posting for this job says workers repair buildings, fences and other structures by hand with tools such as shovels, trowels, hoes and tampers.
The H-2A job posting lists repairing farm buildings, fences and other structures as a hands-on field duty.

There are autonomous robots that inspect fences, but none were found that repair them. Since a software-only agent has no body, it could only help with small parts like looking up materials or repair methods.

Cellular trap sensors such as the Skyhawk Trapmate send an alert to a phone when a trap is triggered. They only send the alert. Someone still has to go to the trap, remove the catch and reset or move it.

In a field trial on dingo foot-hold traps, a satellite or cellular trap-alert system reported 91% of captures. It helps decide which traps to visit but does not do the physical inspection, catch removal or resetting.
Trap-check laws, such as Arizona's daily inspection rule, require the trapper to inspect traps in use. Licensed people handle the inspection, removal of animals and resetting.
In fleshing, the worker drapes the raw pelt over a fleshing beam and pushes fat and meat off with a fleshing knife. It is hands-on manual work with sharp tools, which a software-only agent cannot do.

Trapper-education guides describe fleshing as a physical skill: the knife is used with the right pressure so it doesn't expose hair roots, and all fat has to come off to prevent grease burn. A person has to handle the pelt directly.

State wildlife guidance on processing fur covers skinning and fleshing by hand with knives or draw knives. It names no software or automated digital tool for this step, and no licence is needed for the scraping itself.

M-44 sodium cyanide is a restricted-use pesticide. Users must be trained and certified, warning signs must be posted at the application site, and residents within half a mile must be told in person or by a door tag. That means a licensed human has to carry it out, and some steps are physical.
Some state wildlife agencies, such as Georgia DNR and New Jersey, now let people apply for trapping licences and permits online. An agent could fill in and submit those forms digitally.
Massachusetts trap registration uses a mail-in paper application, and the registration number has to be marked on each trap. Some approval steps are on paper or physical.

Fish reach processors and buyers by physical means: pick-up trucks, boats, lorries, refrigerated trucks, reefer containers and air. Keeping the cold chain intact in transit is a physical job, not a software one.
Fishers who deliver direct need their own refrigerated van to transport the catch, so the core of the task is driving and handling the fish.

The digital side of a delivery (landing reports and fish tickets in eLandings) is mostly done by the receiving processor. The tickets are printed for signature, so this leaves only a small paperwork share an agent could help with.

Maine requires trap/pot gear to carry physical colored marks on buoy lines (for example 4 purple and 1 green in federal waters, with both trawl ends marked) and weak links of 600 lb or less on buoys. The worker has to attach these by hand on the boat or dock.

Massachusetts requires a solid red mark at least 3 ft long in the surface system and red marks no more than 60 ft apart along the line, with breaking-strength limits. The job is rigging rope, floats and weights by hand. Software can only look up the rules.

The rules are about how gear is built and marked, not about having a licensed person sign off. Any crew member can attach the accessories. The real obstacle for AI is the physical work, which a software-only agent cannot do.

Maintenance software such as UpKeep schedules preventive maintenance and recommends service intervals from failure history and sensor data. It also creates work orders with checklists attached. Vendor claims say users build these checklists from templates. No source showed AI writing procedures from scratch. Only the 'recommend or develop procedures' part of the task can be done in software.

HVAC preventive maintenance software provides checklists and seasonal schedules for chillers, air handlers and boilers. People still have to clean, oil parts and change filters by hand at the equipment.

EPA Section 608 certification covers only work that could release refrigerant, such as attaching gauges or adding refrigerant. Routine cleaning, oiling and filter changes generally do not need a licence or a human sign-off.

AI vision and machine-learning inspection is used in jewelry production, but it runs on dedicated cameras and machine controllers built into the production line. A software-only agent cannot pick up and examine a piece.

In jewelry quality control, computer vision and laser measurement can flag defects in metals and stones and check that a design is consistent. This is a promotional source with no accuracy figures. An agent could analyze images and measurements a human captures, but the human still handles the piece with a loupe and gauges.

AI visual inspection systems output a defect class, location and confidence, and compare these to tolerance data to accept or reject a part. An agent could do this comparison against the specification once a human supplies the images or measurements.

Vendors describe AI crew-planning agents that can roster crews, check schedules against qualification, duty-time and union rules, and propose or make reassignments behind approval gates. This covers the scheduling and coordination sub-steps, but these are promotional product pages, not independent evaluations.
AI matching of available, qualified crew to assignments is described as the most mature AI use in 2026 aviation crew scheduling. This source is a vendor blog.

FAA Part 121 requires minimum flight-attendant staffing and on-board positioning for safety and evacuation. Directing attendants in the cabin during operations needs physical human presence, and the certificate holder is accountable for the crew's duties.

Fleet incident apps already guide drivers through accident reporting at the scene. Crashwise uses an AI guide and turns the driver's photos and videos into a standardized digital report that goes to fleet managers. The driver still has to gather the facts at the scene.

AI dashcams such as CameraMatics record video automatically before, during and after an incident, and the companion app supports the claims process. Software can therefore fill in much of the report's evidence and data.

California law makes the driver responsible for filing the SR-1 accident report within 10 days, regardless of fault. An insurance agent, attorney or other representative may file it for the driver, but the account of what happened has to come from the driver.

In early hump yards, brakemen rode cars down the hill and slowed them with hand-operated brakes. Mechanized retarders, controlled manually or by automatic feedback, later replaced this work. So the task is physical, and the automation that exists is trackside machinery, not a software agent.

Modern retarder systems, such as the one at Bailey Yard, set car speed automatically from car weight, distance, wind and temperature. This takes over the speed-control goal through physical yard equipment, not through an AI agent acting by software alone.

Under 49 CFR 218.99 and railroad operating rules, a crewmember physically on site protects and rides equipment during switching moves. The NTSB has urged a ban on riding cars after 14 deaths since 2020.
